messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 78

# Margaret's Careful World

Margaret sits in the waiting room with her hands folded in her lap, her posture impeccable. She's a woman accustomed to precision—in her work examining crime scenes, in how she arranges her home, in the way she speaks. But there's a brittleness to her composure, as though she's holding herself together by force of will.

Three years ago, her younger brother James died suddenly of a ruptured aneurysm. He was 39, fit, with two young children. Margaret had spoken to him on the phone that morning. He'd called about their mother's upcoming birthday party. Nothing seemed wrong. By evening, he was gone.

Margaret remembers the moment the hospital called. She remembers her hands shaking so badly she couldn't hold the phone. She remembers thinking—with the analytical mind that usually serves her well in the morgue—that this couldn't be real. People didn't just stop existing. There were explanations. There were causes. There had to be something that could have been prevented, detected, known.

She threw herself into understanding what happened. She requested the autopsy report. She read the neuropathology findings multiple times, as if repetition might change the outcome or reveal something the medical examiners had missed. Her colleagues at work noticed she was spending longer hours examining cases, cross-referencing, verifying. She couldn't let anything slip through. Not anymore. Not when something so catastrophic had gone undetected in her own family.

Now, Margaret finds herself unable to relax. She checks on her husband repeatedly throughout the day, texting him at work to make sure he's okay. When he doesn't respond immediately, her chest tightens and her mind races through worst-case scenarios. She's become hypervigilant about health—she reads articles about sudden cardiac death, aneurysms, strokes, memorizing symptoms she might have missed in James. She's convinced something is wrong with her own body. Some mornings she wakes with her heart pounding, convinced she's dying, only to realize nothing has actually happened.

Sleep is difficult. She lies awake most nights, her mind cycling through the same thoughts: What if she'd called James more often? What if she'd insisted he get a physical? What if she'd recognized some subtle sign she'd missed? The guilt is relentless, even though the rational part of her—the forensic analyst—knows that no one could have predicted his death.

At work, she's become even more meticulous, though her supervisor has gently mentioned concerns. Margaret notices she's withdrawn from her colleagues. She skips the usual lunch conversations. She can't engage in small talk about weekend plans or family gatherings. When someone mentions their brother or a health scare, she feels her throat constrict. Last week, a junior analyst mentioned her father had chest pain, and Margaret found herself in the bathroom unable to breathe.

She avoids the places she and James used to go. She hasn't visited their mother in months, though they live only forty minutes apart. She tells herself it's because of work, but the truth is more complicated. Being in her mother's house, seeing the empty chair at the dinner table, seeing how her mother's hands shake now—it's unbearable.

Margaret's husband has suggested therapy several times. She's resisted, believing she should be able to manage this herself. She's trained to observe suffering in others, to document it professionally, to remain objective. But she's beginning to understand that her own suffering isn't something she can analyze away. The loss sits in her chest, heavy and immovable, and all the precision in the world cannot undo what happened on that ordinary morning three years ago.
